18Z upper air analysis depicts a well-defined cyclone rotating over 
the Hudson Bay, along with a subtropical ridge, objectively analyzed 
at 598 dam, centered in the southern High Plains. The subtropical 
ridge encompasses the western half of the U.S., while more-sharply 
cyclonic flow is present over the region and northeastward into New 
England. An anticyclonically-curved jet streak, also objectively 
analyzed at nearly 100 kt, arcs around the apex of the subtropical 
ridge before approaching the inflection point of large-scale cyclone 
over far northeastern Canada, with its exit-region advecting over 
the CWA. The respective jetlets of these two synoptic features are 
not phased; however, an intense, shortwave perturbation is embedded 
within the leading edge of the anticyclonically-curved jet streak 
branching southeastward over the Great Lakes, where an organized MCS 
is ongoing across portions of Lake Michigan. This MCS will have 
implications to the forecast across the CWA late tonight into 
Tuesday morning and afternoon.

At the surface, a weak anticyclone was located in the vicinity of 
the Coal Fields in eastern KY, with a warm front progressing 
eastward towards the I-69 corridor. Winds were calm and variable, 
but are expected to transition towards the southwest this evening 
into the nighttime hours while becoming breezy as the warm front 
moves eastward across the region. Southwesterly winds between 10-15 
mph, with gusts up to 20 mph, will be common area-wide by sunrise 
Tuesday due to the large-scale pressure falls associated with the 
system emerging over the CWA late tonight. The low stratus deck 
draped across the CWA earlier this morning has since transitioned 
into a shallow cu field, but large-scale subsidence (capping) will 
preclude any development of showers or thunderstorms for the rest of 
the afternoon across the CWA.

The potential for showers and storms will begin to increase late 
tonight, with the eastern edge of the aforementioned MCS forecast to 
clip the western portions of the CWA across KY, far southeastern OH, 
and far southwestern WV. Forward-propagation of this MCS is already 
underway, and upshear and downshear Corfidi vectors are aligned 
slightly to the right of the mean wind, with enlarged magnitudes at 
around 25 kt and 55 kt, respectively. The main core of the MCS is 
forecast to nosedive southward along the thickness gradient and miss 
the CWA with respect to the bulk of severe-caliber storms; however, 
a couple of strong gusts in excess of 40 mph and heavy rainfall will 
be possible as it clips the western zones late tonight. Weakening of 
the MCS will also be attributed to diabatic stabilization of the 
airmass and the eventual forward-surging of outflow from the leading 
edge of convection, with an expectation for a quick progression as a 
more-substantial shortwave trough splitting off from the cyclone 
wobbling over the Hudson Bay trails behind while digging into the 
Great Lakes. That said, remnant outflow boundaries may propagate 
into the CWA ahead of the secondary shortwave trough digging 
southeastward towards the region during the predawn hours Tuesday. 

Vigorous and moist, isentropic ascent will overspread the CWA ahead 
of this shortwave trough, with widespread showers and storms 
forecast to evolve and advect towards the southeast across the CWA 
prior to and after sunrise. The mean convective movement associated 
with the mid-to-late-morning clusters of storms will be governed 
largely by advection, as the core(s) of the 250 mb and 500 mb jet 
streaks, at or around 90 kt and 50 kt, respectively, translate over 
the CWA amidst an unfavorable alignment of the shear vectors to 
allow for upwind propagation. The remnant outflow(s) may serve as a 
foci for localized enhancements to the cellular clusters, especially 
given the vigor of moist, isentropic ascent as the synoptic cold 
front moves in from the northwest. Efficient rainfall is expected 
due to warm-cloud depths of 15-16 kft AGL and wet-bulb zero heights 
above 14 kft. Therefore, swaths of heavy rainfall are a certainty 
with the mid-to-late-morning episode of convection, but the 
progressive, southeastward movement is forecast to keep the flash 
flooding potential localized due to the magnitude of the mean wind 
vectors approaching 40 kt. A few strong wind gusts in the 30-40 mph 
range cannot be ruled out near and after sunrise Tuesday, but the 
columns should otherwise be too moist to warrant the production of 
strong, convective wind gusts. 

Storm chances heading into Tuesday afternoon following this 
secondary convective episode remain less certain. It appears that at 
least isolated-to-widely-scattered, elevated showers and storms will 
be possible as a smaller-scale, closed cyclone forms within the 
shortwave trough digging into NY. Northwesterly flow will maximize
